report:
## Conclusion

The claim is **well-supported by strong clinical evidence**. Abaloparatide, an anabolic PTH1-receptor-related peptide analog, significantly reduces the risk of new vertebral fractures (as well as nonvertebral fractures) in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis.

The pivotal evidence comes from the **ACTIVE trial**, a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 3 study of over 2,000 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis. Compared with placebo, 18 months of daily subcutaneous abaloparatide (80 mcg) reduced new vertebral fracture risk by approximately 86%, and also lowered nonvertebral fracture risk, with effects consistent across age, BMD, and prior fracture history (JAMA, 2016; PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27533157/; https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2544640). These benefits were durable through the 43-month ACTIVE/ACTIVExtend extension, including in high-risk subgroups (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6916366/).

A subsequent network meta-analysis comparing abaloparatide to other approved osteoporosis therapies (bisphosphonates, denosumab, teriparatide, raloxifene) found abaloparatide among the most effective agents for reducing both vertebral and nonvertebral fracture risk (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/332256197).

This evidence base underpins the FDA-approved product labeling for Tymlos (abaloparatide), which explicitly states that in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, the drug "reduces the risk of vertebral and nonvertebral fractures," with benefit consistent regardless of age, years since menopause, or baseline BMD (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2017/208743lbl.pdf).

**Bottom line:** Randomized controlled trial data, long-term extension data, network meta-analyses, and FDA regulatory labeling all converge to support that abaloparatide reduces vertebral fracture risk in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis. The claim is accurate.
